text:
Chamomile (Romashka аптечная) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik

In the monastery herbals [travniki] of the Russian Orthodox tradition, chamomile [Romashka аптечная] was esteemed as one of the foremost healing plants, employed to calm inflammation of the stomach and bowels, to ease spasmodic pain of the belly, and to drive out putrid fevers [gnilostnye likhoradki]. Siberian folk healers and monastery physicians alike prepared warm infusions of the dried flower heads to treat melancholy, nervous agitation, and sleeplessness, associating the plant's golden centre with solar, purifying virtue in the manner of Byzantine humoural medicine. Externally, chamomile decoctions were applied as washes and compresses for festering wounds, skin eruptions, and inflammation of the eyes, a practice noted in both Central Asian [tibb] and native Siberian healing lore absorbed into the monastic manuscript tradition.

Preparation: {'method': 'Infusion [nastoi]: One to two tablespoons [Russian: lozhka] of dried chamomile flower heads steeped in one cup [chashka] of freshly boiled water for 15–20 minutes, covered to retain volatile oils; strained and taken warm. Decoction [otvar] for external use: a stronger preparation of 3–4 tablespoons per litre of water, simmered gently for 10 minutes, cooled, and applied as a wash or compress.', 'dosage': 'Internal: one cup of warm infusion taken two to three times daily before meals for digestive complaints; at bedtime for sleeplessness and nervous agitation. External: applied as needed to affected skin or eyes.', 'form': 'Infusion (internal); decoction (external wash/compress)'}
Indication: ['Inflammation of the stomach and intestines [gastritis, enteritis]', 'Spasmodic abdominal pain [koliki]', 'Putrid and intermittent fevers [gnilostnye i peremezhaushchiesia likhoradki]', 'Nervous agitation and melancholy [toska, nervnoe razdrazhenie]', 'Sleeplessness [bessonnitsa]', 'Festering wounds and skin eruptions [gnoinye rany, kozhnye vysypaniya]', 'Inflammation of the eyes [vospalenie glaz]']

Original: Ромашка аптечная (Romashka aptechnaya) — Matricaria chamomilla L. [Source: Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik, 17th–18th century manuscript tradition]
title: Chamomile (Romashka аптечная) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik

text:
St John's Wort — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik (17th–18th century)

Known in Russian monastic medicine as 'Зверобой' [lit. 'beast-slayer'], this herb was regarded as one of the most versatile and sacred of the healing plants preserved in Orthodox monastery herbariums, where monks employed it chiefly for its powers against melancholy, wounded flesh, and disorders of the bowel. In Slavic folk tradition, it was held to ward off evil spirits and afflictions of the nervous spirit [nervnoe rastroenie], and Siberian practitioners used it alongside shamanic preparations for melancholic states [toska] and sleeplessness, beliefs that blended into the monastery tradition through Central Asian and Siberian plant knowledge absorbed along pilgrimage and trade routes. The plant's oil-bearing perforated leaves — visible as translucent dots when held to light — were considered evidence of divine marking, lending it particular authority in monastic wound-healing and as a bitter tonic for the stomach and liver.

Original: Зверобой продырявленный (Zveroboi prodyrávlennyj) — Hypericum perforatum L.
title: St John's Wort — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik (17th–18th century)

text:
Valerian — Traditional Russian Monastery Herbal Medicine

Valerian [Валериана лекарственная] was among the most prized [tselyebnye] or 'healing' herbs in the Orthodox monastery tradition, where monks cultivated and dispensed it primarily as a remedy for disturbances of the mind and spirit — what the manuscripts term 'unquiet of the heart' [nespokoystviye serdtsa] and 'trembling of the limbs.' Monastic healers prepared root decoctions to calm the afflicted, aid disordered sleep, and ease the 'falling sickness' [paduchaya bolezn', i.e., epilepsy], drawing on Byzantine medical inheritance as well as Siberian folk practice in which Valerian root was burned as a smoke remedy to dispel evil spirits believed responsible for seizures and madness. The root was also administered internally to relieve pains of the stomach and intestines, suppress palpitations of the heart [bienie serdtsa], and restore composure to those suffering from grief, fright, or prolonged illness.

Preparation: The dried root of Valerian was typically prepared as a water decoction [otvar]: roots were chopped or crushed, simmered gently in water (ratio approximately one part root to ten parts water) for fifteen to twenty minutes, then strained and administered warm in small cups [chashki] several times daily. Alcohol tinctures [nastoyka na spirtu] were also recorded in later monastery manuscripts, prepared by steeping dried root in grain spirit for seven to fourteen days. For Siberian shamanic-adjacent folk uses, dried root or root chips were sometimes burned on coals and the smoke inhaled or directed over the patient.
Indication: Insomnia and disordered sleep; nervous agitation and anxiety ('unquiet of the heart'); epilepsy ('falling sickness' [paduchaya bolezn']); palpitations of the heart; stomach and intestinal pain; nervous exhaustion from grief or fright; spirit-caused illness in Siberian folk practice.

Original: Валериана лекарственная (Valeriana officinalis) — Transliteration: Valeriana lekarstvennaya. Source: Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik (травник), 17th–18th century herbal medicine tradition, blending Byzantine, Central Asian, and native Siberian plant knowledge.
title: Valerian — Traditional Russian Monastery Herbal Medicine

text:
Calendula (Pot Marigold) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Uses

In the Russian Orthodox monastery herbal [travnik] tradition of the 17th–18th centuries, Calendula [Календула лекарственная] was esteemed above all as a wound herb and purifier of the blood, applied both inwardly and outwardly for the healing of festering sores, ulcers of the skin, and inflammation of the inner organs. Monastic physicians prepared decoctions of the dried flower heads to treat disorders of the liver, spleen, and stomach, as well as to ease fevers and expel harmful humours [vrednyye soki, lit. 'harmful juices'] from the body. In Siberian folk practice, where Orthodox monastery medicine mingled with indigenous plant knowledge, the blossoms were also laid upon the temples and brow to relieve headache, and the expressed juice was dropped into inflamed eyes.

Preparation: Decoction [otvar]: one to two tablespoons of dried flower heads [tsvetochnye korzinki] simmered in two cups (approximately 400–500 ml) of water for ten to fifteen minutes, strained, and taken warm in doses of one half-cup two to three times daily before meals. For external application, a stronger decoction was prepared using a double quantity of flowers and applied as a warm compress or wash to wounds and skin lesions. A cold infusion [nastoy] was also used for eye complaints: a teaspoon of dried flowers steeped in one cup of boiled water for thirty minutes, strained through fine cloth, and applied as an eyewash.
Indication: ['Festering wounds and skin ulcers [gnoynyye rany i yazvy]', 'Inflammation of the liver, spleen, and stomach', 'Fever and systemic inflammation', 'Headache (external topical application)', 'Eye inflammation and irritation (ophthalmic wash)', 'Blood impurity [zasoryoniye krovi] — humoral concept']

Original: Календула лекарственная (Kalendula lekarstvennaya) — Calendula officinalis L.
title: Calendula (Pot Marigold) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Uses

text:
Yarrow — Traditional Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

Yarrow [тысячелистник, lit. 'thousand-leafed'] was among the most esteemed wound herbs of the Russian Orthodox monastery tradition, prized above all for its power to staunch bleeding [кровоостанавливающее действие] from cuts, battle wounds, and internal hemorrhage. Monastery physicians prescribed it in decoction for disorders of the stomach and bowels — including cramps, dysentery, and sluggish digestion — drawing on both Byzantine medical texts transmitted through Athonite monasteries and native Slavic folk knowledge. In Siberian and trans-Ural regions, where shamanic plant knowledge was absorbed into syncretic Orthodox practice, yarrow was additionally employed as a febrifuge [жаропонижающее], a remedy for painful menstruation, and a general tonic for debility following prolonged illness.

Preparation: Standard monastery preparation: aerial parts (flowering tops and leaves) harvested at full bloom (June–August), dried in shade. Decoction [отвар]: 1 tablespoon dried herb to 1 cup (200 ml) boiling water, simmered 10–15 minutes, strained, taken warm in doses of ½ cup two to three times daily before meals. Cold infusion [настой] also recorded for external wound-washing. Tincture in monastery wine or grain spirit occasionally noted for febrifuge use in colder climates.
Indication: Hemostasis (external and internal bleeding); gastric and intestinal disorders (cramps, dysentery, poor digestion); fever (febrifuge); dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation); general debility and convalescence.

Original: Тысячелистник обыкновенный (transliteration: Tysyachelistnik obyknovennyy) — Achillea millefolium L. Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik (травник), 17th–18th century tradition.
title: Yarrow — Traditional Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

text:
Plantain (Plantago major) — Russian Monastery Herbal Tradition

Known in the monastery healing tradition as 'Podorozhnik' [lit. 'road-follower,' named for its growth along travelled paths], the great plantain was among the most widely employed vulnerary [wound-healing] herbs in both Orthodox monastic pharmacy and Siberian folk medicine. Monks prepared it for the cleansing of festering wounds, the staunching of blood, the relief of coughs and chest ailments, and the soothing of inflammation of the stomach and bowels. In Siberian shamanic-adjacent folk practice, the fresh leaf was applied directly to snakebite and insect sting, and the seed mucilage [sliz semyan] was taken internally to ease 'hot' fevers and restore the 'moistness' of the body in the humoral sense inherited from Byzantine medical writings.

Preparation: Fresh leaves were bruised and bound directly to wounds or ulcers [ulcery, yazvy] as a poultice, renewed twice daily. For internal use, a decoction [otvar] was prepared by simmering one handful of dried leaves in two cups of water for 15–20 minutes, strained, and taken in doses of one small cup [charka] two to three times daily before meals. The seeds were soaked overnight in cold water to produce a mucilaginous infusion [slizisty nastoy] taken by the spoonful for cough and gastric irritation. Tincture [nastoyка] in monastery practice sometimes employed spirits [vino] infused with dried leaf for longer preservation.
Indication: Wounds, ulcers, and festering sores (vulnerary); cough, bronchial irritation, and chest congestion (expectorant); gastric and intestinal inflammation, diarrhea (demulcent, antidiarrheal); fever (febrifuge); snakebite and insect sting (topical antivenomous folk use); headache (topical poultice to the temples, noted in some manuscript variants).

Original: Подорожник большой (Podorozhnik bol'shoy) — Plantago major L. [From the Russian Orthodox monastery travnik (травник), 17th–18th century manuscript tradition.]
title: Plantain (Plantago major) — Russian Monastery Herbal Tradition

text:
Nettle (Крапива двудомная) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

Nettle [крапива] was among the most widely employed medicinal herbs in Russian Orthodox monastery medicine, valued for its capacity to stanch bleeding [кровоостанавливающее], fortify the blood, and stimulate the liver and kidneys. Monastery healers and Siberian folk practitioners alike administered nettle decoctions to treat joint afflictions [ломота в суставах], skin eruptions, and general bodily weakness, while fresh leaves were applied directly to rheumatic limbs — a practice also recorded in shamanic Siberian traditions as a means of driving illness from the body through the stinging sensation [уртикация, or urtication]. The seeds and roots were additionally held to promote hair growth and combat hair loss, and the expressed juice of young spring shoots was taken internally as a tonic [общеукрепляющее] to restore vitality after winter.

Preparation: {'decoction': 'One to two tablespoons of dried nettle leaf or root boiled in one cup (approximately 200 ml) of water for 10–15 minutes; strained and taken warm, two to three times daily before meals.', 'infusion': 'One tablespoon of dried leaves steeped in boiling water for 20 minutes; used internally for blood-fortifying and diuretic [мочегонное] effect.', 'fresh_application': 'Fresh green leaves bundled and applied directly to rheumatic or painful joints [urtication]; also, fresh spring shoot juice pressed and taken in doses of one to two tablespoons daily as a seasonal tonic.', 'tincture': 'Seeds macerated in alcohol or honey-wine [медовуха] for external application to the scalp to encourage hair growth.', 'dosage_notes': 'Internal decoctions typically taken in courses of 14–21 days; fresh juice restricted to spring harvest of young shoots only.'}
Indication: ['hemorrhage and excessive menstrual bleeding [кровотечение]', 'anemia and blood deficiency [малокровие]', 'rheumatism and joint pain [ломота в суставах]', 'skin disorders and eruptions [кожные высыпания]', 'liver and kidney complaints', 'general debility and post-winter weakness', 'hair loss and scalp conditions', 'urinary tract complaints [мочегонное применение]']

Original: Крапива двудомная (Krapiva dvudomnaya) — Urtica dioica L. Источник: Русский православный монастырский травник, XVII–XVIII вв.
title: Nettle (Крапива двудомная) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

text:
Birch (Betula pendula) — Traditional Russian Monastery Herbal Medicine

The weeping birch [Берёза повислая] was among the most revered medicinal trees in Russian Orthodox monastery medicine and Siberian folk tradition. Its leaves, buds, bark, and sap [берёзовый сок] were employed to treat kidney and bladder ailments, joint inflammation [ломота в суставах], skin eruptions, and fevers, with the tree regarded in some Siberian shamanic contexts as a sacred axis between the earthly and spirit worlds. Monastery herbalists [травники] prescribed birch preparations for purifying the blood [очищение крови], expelling worms, easing gout [подагра], and as a diuretic [мочегонное средство], while birch tar [дёготь] was applied externally to treat eczema, scabies, and infected wounds.

Preparation: Leaf and bud infusion [настой]: steep 1–2 tablespoons of dried young leaves or buds in 250 ml boiling water for 20–30 minutes; strain and drink warm, 100 ml three times daily as a diuretic and blood-purifier. Bark decoction [отвар коры]: simmer dried inner bark (15 g) in 500 ml water for 20 minutes; used externally as a wash for skin conditions or taken internally in small doses for fevers and joint pain. Birch sap [берёзовый сок]: drunk fresh, 200–500 ml daily in spring as a general tonic. Birch tar [дёготь]: applied directly or mixed with lard [свиной жир] as an ointment [мазь] for eczema, scabies, and infected wounds.
Indication: Kidney and bladder disorders (diuretic); joint inflammation and gout [подагра]; skin diseases including eczema, scabies, and infected wounds; intestinal parasites (anthelmintic); fevers; blood impurities [нечистота крови]; general springtime tonic and restorative.

Original: Берёза повислая (Beryoza povislaya) — Betula pendula. Источник: Русский православный монастырский травник, XVII–XVIII века.
title: Birch (Betula pendula) — Traditional Russian Monastery Herbal Medicine

text:
Linden / Lime Flower (Tilia cordata) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

The small-leaved linden [липа сердцелистная], long revered within Orthodox monastery gardens and Siberian folk healing alike, was employed principally as a sudorific [потогонное] and febrifuge, its flowers gathered at midsummer and prepared as a hot infusion to break fevers, expel catarrh, and ease inflammation of the chest and throat. Monastery herbalists further prescribed linden-flower water as a gentle antispasmodic for the heart and nerves, regarding the sweetly scented blossom as a gift of divine mercy suited to calming night agitations, palpitations, and melancholic humours [уныние]. In Siberian and West Siberian folk practice the inner bark [луб] was additionally used, boiled into a thick decoction for application to burns, scalds, and erysipelas of the skin, while the charcoal of the wood served as an internal remedy for dysentery and intestinal putrefaction.

Preparation: {'infusion': 'Dried linden flowers (цветки липы): 1–2 tablespoons per cup of boiling water; steeped covered for 15–20 minutes; consumed hot, 2–3 cups per day at onset of fever or chill, to promote perspiration [потогонный эффект].', 'decoction_bark': 'Inner bark (луб): a small handful simmered in water for 20–30 minutes; strained and applied warm as a compress or wash to burns, erysipelas, or inflamed skin.', 'charcoal': 'Wood charcoal of linden, ground fine and taken internally in small doses (a pinch or two dissolved in water) for dysentery and intestinal complaints.', 'condition': ['Fever and influenza [горячка, лихорадка]', 'Catarrh and inflammation of the throat and chest', 'Nervous palpitations and cardiac spasm [сердцебиение]', 'Melancholy and night agitation [уныние, бессонница]', 'Burns, scalds, and erysipelas (external bark decoction)', 'Dysentery and intestinal putrefaction (linden charcoal)']}
Indication: ['Fever / influenza', 'Upper respiratory catarrh', 'Cardiac palpitations and nervous spasm', 'Melancholia and insomnia', 'Burns and erysipelas (topical)', 'Dysentery and intestinal disorder (charcoal preparation)']

Original: Липа сердцелистная (Lipa serdtselistnaya) — Tilia cordata Mill. Monastery Travnik (травник), 17th–18th century.
title: Linden / Lime Flower (Tilia cordata) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

text:
Elecampane (Девясил высокий) — Traditional Russian Monastery and Folk Medicinal Uses

Elecampane [Девясил высокий, lit. 'nine strengths high'], long revered in Russian Orthodox monastery medicine, was considered among the most potent of healing roots, credited with restoring vitality across nine bodily systems — hence its folk name. The root [корень девясила] was employed in decoctions to treat disorders of the chest and lungs, persistent coughs, and shortness of breath, and was additionally prescribed for afflictions of the stomach and bowels, including sluggish digestion, griping [koliki], and parasitic worms. In Siberian shamanic and folk traditions running parallel to monastery practice, the dried root was burned or carried as a protective amulet, while the medicinal preparations were also applied externally to skin eruptions [korosty], scrofulous sores [skrofuly], and joint pains [sustavnye boli].

Preparation: {'method': 'Decoction [otvar] of dried root: 1–2 tablespoons (approximately 15–30 g) of coarsely chopped dried root simmered in 500 ml of water for 15–20 minutes, then strained and cooled. Also prepared as a cold-water infusion [nastoy na kholodnoy vode] steeped overnight for gentler extraction of mucilaginous compounds. Tincture [nastoyка] in aquavit or grain spirit was used for external application to skin and joint conditions.', 'dosage': 'Decoction: one-half cup [polstakana, approx. 100 ml] taken warm, two to three times daily before meals. Tincture: applied externally by cloth compress [kompres] to affected areas.'}
Indication: ["Chronic cough [kashel'] and pulmonary complaints", 'Shortness of breath and bronchial congestion', 'Disorders of digestion and stomach griping [koliki]', 'Intestinal parasites and worms [glisty]', 'Skin eruptions and scrofulous sores [skrofuly, korosty]', 'Joint pain and rheumatic complaints [sustavnye boli]']

Original: Девясил высокий (Devyasil vysokiy) — Inula helenium L. Source: Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik (травник), 17th–18th century herbal medicine tradition. Context: Slavic folk medicine preserved in monastery manuscripts, blending Byzantine, Central Asian, and native Siberian plant knowledge.
title: Elecampane (Девясил высокий) — Traditional Russian Monastery and Folk Medicinal Uses

text:
Wormwood (Полынь горькая) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik

Wormwood [Polyn' gor'kaya], long esteemed in Orthodox monastery medicine, was prescribed chiefly as a bitter tonic [горечь] to stimulate digestion, expel intestinal worms [глисты], and fortify a weakened stomach. Monastery healers also applied wormwood externally as a poultice or wash to cleanse festering wounds, relieve joint pain [ломота], and drive away fevers thought to arise from corrupt humors or 'cold miasma' [студёный воздух]. In Siberian folk and shamanic contexts the plant was burned as a purifying smoke [окуривание] to ward off evil spirits and epidemic sickness, a practice that overlapped with its genuine antiseptic properties and was tacitly tolerated within the monastery healing tradition.

Preparation: Three primary forms are attested in the Travnik tradition: (1) Decoction [отвар] — 1–2 tablespoons of dried aerial herb simmered in 1 cup (approximately 250 ml) of water for 10–15 minutes, strained and taken in doses of 1–2 tablespoons before meals to stimulate appetite and digestion. (2) Cold infusion [настой] — herb steeped in cold water overnight, taken in small doses as an anthelmintic. (3) External poultice — fresh or rehydrated herb applied directly to wounds or aching joints, bound with linen cloth. Fumigation [окуривание] employed dried stems burned on embers in enclosed spaces during epidemic illness.
Indication: Digestive weakness and loss of appetite; intestinal worm infestation [helminthiasis]; festering or slow-healing wounds; rheumatic joint pain [ломота]; intermittent fever; epidemic illness (preventive fumigation); general debility attributed to cold or corrupt humors.

Original: Полынь горькая (Polyn' gor'kaya) — Artemisia absinthium L. Источник: Русский православный монастырский травник, XVII–XVIII вв.
title: Wormwood (Полынь горькая) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik

text:
Comfrey (Окопник лекарственный) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik

Known in the monastery tradition as Окопник ('the consolidator' or 'trench-herb'), this root was esteemed above all for its power to knit broken bones, mend torn sinews, and close deep wounds — properties attributed in Orthodox herbal commentary to the abundant [slizistye veshchestva] (mucilaginous substances) residing in its thick, blackened root. Monastery physicians prepared the root as a thick decoction or a poultice applied directly to fractures, sprains, and ulcerated skin, while Siberian folk healers additionally employed the fresh bruised leaf as an emergency field dressing for bleeding cuts and inflamed joints. In some manuscript traditions, an internal decoction of the dried root was administered cautiously for coughs, hoarseness, and complaints of the chest [grudnye bolezni], reflecting the Byzantine-derived doctrine that the same mucilage that seals external wounds could soothe and coat the inflamed passages within.

Preparation: {'decoction': 'Dried root (30–60 g) simmered in water (1 litre) for 20–30 minutes, strained, and taken internally in small cups (approximately 100 ml) two to three times daily for chest and digestive complaints. Externally, the strained decoction was applied as a warm compress or the root was ground to a paste and bound over fractures and wounds with linen cloth.', 'poultice': 'Fresh or rehydrated dried root was grated or pounded and applied directly to the affected area, covered with cloth and changed twice daily.', 'tincture': 'Less commonly, the root was macerated in wine or spirit [spirtovoye nastaivaniye] for several weeks and rubbed into painful joints and bruised limbs.', 'dosage_notes': 'Internal use was typically limited in duration; monastery texts caution against prolonged internal administration, consistent with modern awareness of pyrrolizidine alkaloid content.'}
Indication: ['Fractures and broken bones [perelomy kostey]', 'Sprains and torn ligaments [rastyazheniya i razryvy svyazok]', 'Deep or slow-healing wounds and ulcers [yazvy i gnoynyye rany]', 'Inflammation of joints [vospaleniye sustavov]', "Cough, hoarseness, and chest complaints [grudnye bolezni, kashel', khripota]", 'Digestive inflammation and gastric ulcer [vospaleniye zheludka]']

Original: Окопник лекарственный (Okopnik lekarstvennyy) — Symphytum officinale L. Source: Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik (травник), 17th–18th century manuscript tradition. Context: Slavic folk medicine preserved in monastery herbals, synthesizing Byzantine humoral theory, Central Asian materia medica, and native Siberian plant knowledge.
title: Comfrey (Окопник лекарственный) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik

text:
Field Horsetail (Хвощ полевой) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik

Field horsetail [Хвощ полевой, lit. 'field tail'], a wetland and meadow plant widely documented in Russian Orthodox monastery herbal manuscripts of the 17th–18th centuries, was employed as a diuretic [мочегонное], haemostatic [кровоостанавливающее], and blood-purifying [очищающее кровь] remedy. Monastery healers prepared decoctions of the dried aerial stems to treat disorders of the kidneys and bladder, urinary retention, oedema of the limbs, and pulmonary haemorrhage; in the Siberian folk tradition the plant was additionally associated with the cleansing of 'bad blood' and the treatment of skin eruptions and festering wounds. Some manuscript sources reflect a convergence with Byzantine humoral medicine, recommending horsetail to 'dry out excess moisture' [осушить лишнюю влагу] in the body, while Siberian shamanic-adjacent folk practice valued the plant's astringent properties for stanching internal and external bleeding.

Preparation: {'method': 'Decoction [отвар] of dried aerial stems (sterile green shoots harvested in summer): simmer 1–2 tablespoons (approx. 10–15 g) of dried herb in 500 ml of water for 15–20 minutes; strain. Alternatively prepared as a cold-water infusion [настой] steeped overnight. Tincture in wine or aqua vitae [водка] also recorded in some monastery sources for wound-washing and external application.', 'dosage': 'Decoction taken internally in doses of ½ cup (approx. 100–125 ml) two to three times daily before meals for urinary and oedematous complaints; applied externally as a wash or compress for skin lesions and wounds.', 'frequency': 'Two to three times daily internally; topical application as needed.'}
Indication: ['Kidney and bladder disorders [болезни почек и мочевого пузыря]', 'Urinary retention and dysuria', 'Oedema / dropsy [водянка]', 'Pulmonary haemorrhage [лёгочное кровотечение]', 'External bleeding and festering wounds', 'Skin eruptions and dermatological complaints', "General 'blood impurity' [нечистота крови] — humoral category"]

Original: Хвощ полевой (Khvoshch polevoy) — Equisetum arvense. Травник монастырский, XVII–XVIII вв. Растение болотное и луговое, употребляемое в народной и монастырской медицине как мочегонное, кровоостанавливающее и очищающее средство.
title: Field Horsetail (Хвощ полевой) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik

text:
Celandine (Chelidonium majus) in Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

Celandine [Чистотел большой, lit. 'great purifier'], long esteemed in Orthodox monastery medicine, was principally employed as a [желчегонное] cholagogue and a [противосудорожное] antispasmodic remedy, applied both internally and externally for the purification of the blood and the driving out of 'corrupt humours' [порченые соки] from the body. The fresh acrid yellow-orange latex [млечный сок] of the stem was applied directly to warts, papillomas, skin ulcers, and fungal afflictions of the flesh, a practice recorded across monastery herbals and corroborated in Siberian shamanic tradition, where the plant was considered to carry a 'burning spiritual force' [жгучая духовная сила] capable of dissolving unclean growths. Decoctions of the aerial parts were administered internally for disorders of the liver, gallbladder, and spleen, for jaundice [желтуха], and for convulsive and epileptic episodes [падучая болезнь, lit. 'the falling sickness'], reflecting the Byzantine humoral inheritance mediated through Slavic monastic copyists.

Preparation: External use: Fresh latex [млечный сок] expressed directly from the broken stem was dabbed onto warts, skin growths, and ulcerated lesions once or twice daily until resolution. Internal use: A decoction [отвар] was prepared from 1–2 tablespoons of dried aerial herb per 500 ml of water, simmered gently for 10–15 minutes and strained; administered in doses of 1–2 tablespoons (15–30 ml) two to three times daily before meals. Tincture [настойка] on 40° spirit in a ratio of 1:10 was also recorded, taken in drops (5–10 drops in water) for hepatic and spasmodic complaints. Caution against overdose [передозировка] is noted in several manuscript sources, as excess causes nausea, intestinal irritation, and narcotic stupor.
Indication: ['Warts and papillomas', 'Skin ulcers and fungal skin afflictions', 'Liver and gallbladder disorders', 'Jaundice [желтуха]', 'Spleen disorders', 'Convulsions and epilepsy [падучая болезнь]', "Blood impurity / 'corrupt humours' [порченые соки]"]

Original: Чистотел большой (Chistotel bolshoy) — Chelidonium majus L. [Source: Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik (травник), 17th–18th century herbal medicine tradition. Slavic folk medicine preserved in monastery manuscripts, blending Byzantine, Central Asian, and native Siberian plant knowledge.]
title: Celandine (Chelidonium majus) in Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

text:
Motherwort (Пустырник сердечный) — Heart and Nervous Ailments

Motherwort [pustyrnik serdechnyy, lit. 'heart wasteland-herb'] was employed extensively in Orthodox monastery medicine as a primary remedy for disordered heartbeat, palpitations, and general weakness of the heart organ. The herb and its flowers were administered in decoction form to those suffering from the 'falling sickness' [epilepsy], chronic sleeplessness, and nervous agitation of the spirit — a condition the monastery physicians understood as affliction of both body and soul. In traditions drawing on Siberian and Central Asian folk knowledge absorbed into the monastery herbal corpus, motherwort was also prescribed for uterine complaints [zhenskiye nedugi chreva, lit. 'women's ailments of the womb'], including painful or irregular menses and postpartum weakness.

Preparation: Decoction [otvar] of dried aerial herb and flowers: a small handful of dried herb steeped in boiled water, taken warm in measured doses two to three times daily. Tincture preparations in aqueous spirit [vodka or grain spirit] were also noted in later monastery sources for heart and nervous complaints. Dosage was calibrated to patient constitution, with monastery physicians cautioning restraint in quantity.
Indication: Cardiac palpitations and weakness of the heart; epilepsy and convulsive disorders ['falling sickness']; insomnia and nervous agitation; uterine complaints including painful menstruation and postpartum recovery.

Original: Пустырник сердечный (Pustyrnik serdechnyy) — Leonurus cardiaca. Растение пустырника употребляется в монастырской медицине для успокоения сердечного биения, укрепления немощного сердца, и при великой тревоге духа. Отвар из травы и цветов даётся страждущим от падучей болезни, от бессонницы, и от женских недугов чрева.
title: Motherwort (Пустырник сердечный) — Heart and Nervous Ailments

text:
Bearberry (Толокнянка обыкновенная) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

Bearberry [толокнянка], known in monastery herbals as a purifying herb of the northern forests, was widely employed by Orthodox monks and Siberian folk healers alike for afflictions of the bladder and kidneys, being understood to cleanse the urinary passages and reduce inflammatory heat [воспалительный жар] in those organs. Decoctions of the dried leaves were administered to patients suffering from difficulty or pain in urination, dropsy [водянка], and gravel [почечный песок — kidney sand], with the plant's astringent and diuretic qualities noted by monastic physicians as particularly suited to cold, damp constitutions common in northern climates. In Siberian shamanic-adjacent folk practice, bearberry was additionally associated with spiritual purification and was sometimes incorporated into preparations intended to fortify the body against disease during harsh winters, reflecting the blending of indigenous Siberian herbalism with the Orthodox monastic healing tradition.

Original: Толокнянка обыкновенная (transliteration: Toloknyanka obyknovennaya) — Arctostaphylos uva-ursi. [Source: Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik, 17th–18th century manuscript tradition. Slavic folk medicine, blending Byzantine, Central Asian, and native Siberian plant knowledge.]
title: Bearberry (Толокнянка обыкновенная) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

text:
Cowberry / Lingonberry (Брусника) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik

The cowberry [брусника], known in monastery medicine as a 'cleansing and strengthening berry of the northern forests,' was employed extensively in Russian Orthodox herbal practice for its astringent, diuretic, and antiseptic properties. Decoctions of the leaves were prescribed for ailments of the kidneys and bladder, for [камчужная болезнь] rheumatic and gouty complaints, and for fevers attended by excessive thirst; the berries themselves, preserved in water [мочёная брусника, 'soaked cowberry'], were recommended to purify the blood and restore strength to the weakened. In Siberian folk and shamanic tradition the plant was likewise prized as a remedy against scurvy [цинга], and monastery physicians noted its use among northern peoples to ward off putrefaction of the gums and general bodily corruption arising from poor winter diet.

Preparation: Leaf decoction: dried cowberry leaves [листья брусники] simmered in water and administered internally for kidney, bladder, and rheumatic complaints. Soaked berries [мочёная брусника]: whole ripe berries submerged in cold spring water and kept in a cool cellar; consumed as a daily food-medicine against scurvy and to 'purify the blood' through the winter months.
Indication: Kidney and bladder complaints (diuretic); rheumatism and gout [камчужная болезнь]; fever with thirst; scurvy [цинга]; putrefaction of the gums; general debility arising from nutritional deficiency in winter.

Original: Брусника (Brusnika) — Vaccinium vitis-idaea L. Российский монастырский травник, XVII–XVIII вв. [Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal, 17th–18th century]
title: Cowberry / Lingonberry (Брусника) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik

text:
Cloudberry (Морошка) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

The fruit, leaf, and root of the cloudberry [морошка] are employed in folk medicine and monastery herbals [травники] as a remedy for urinary stone disease [мочекаменная болезнь], scurvy [цинга], cold ailments [простуда], and inflammation of the internal organs. Siberian healers [знахари] and monastery physicians [монастырские лекари] prized the cloudberry for its fever-reducing [жаропонижающее] and diuretic [мочегонное] properties. In the Orthodox monastery tradition, decoctions of the leaf and root were administered to monks suffering from kidney complaints, while the fresh or preserved fruit was given to counter scurvy during long northern winters, its high vitamin C content being understood empirically if not yet named as such.

Preparation: {'method': 'Decoction [отвар] of dried cloudberry leaves and root: 1–2 tablespoons of dried leaf material boiled in 500 ml of water for 10–15 minutes, strained, and taken in doses of one cup [approximately 200 ml] two to three times daily. Fresh or preserved [мочёная] fruit consumed freely as food-medicine, especially in winter, against scurvy. Infusion [настой] of leaves steeped in boiled water for 30 minutes also recorded for milder diuretic and anti-inflammatory use.', 'dosage': 'Decoction: ~200 ml, 2–3 times daily. Fresh fruit: ad libitum as dietary supplement.', 'form': 'Decoction (отвар), infusion (настой), fresh or preserved fruit'}
Indication: ['Urinary stone disease [мочекаменная болезнь] / nephrolithiasis', 'Scurvy [цинга] / vitamin C deficiency', 'Febrile illness / fever [жар, лихорадка]', 'Inflammation of internal organs [воспаление внутренних органов]', 'Common cold and upper respiratory ailments [простуда]', 'Edema / fluid retention (diuretic use)']

Original: Морошка (Moroshka) — Rubus chamaemorus. Плод, лист и корень морошки употребляются в народной медицине и монастырских травниках как средство от мочекаменной болезни, цинги, простуды и воспалений внутренних органов. Сибирские знахари и монастырские лекари ценили морошку за жаропонижающие и мочегонные свойства.
title: Cloudberry (Морошка) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

text:
Sea Buckthorn (Облепиха крушиновидная) — Monastery and Folk Medicinal Uses

Sea buckthorn was esteemed in Russian Orthodox monastery medicine as a potent [vseistselelyayushchee] all-healing remedy, its bright orange berries and leaves employed to strengthen the body against wasting sickness [iznurenie], heal burns and festering wounds of the skin, and fortify the stomach against flux [ponos] and disorders of digestion. Siberian and Central Asian folk healers, whose knowledge filtered into the monastery travnik tradition via the eastward expansion of Orthodox missions, applied the expressed berry oil [масло облепихи, maslo oblepikhi] directly to scorched or ulcerated flesh, holding it to be superior to any other salve for the rapid closing of wounds. The berries, rich in a golden-red oil later identified with vitamin-bearing compounds, were also administered internally to relieve cough, hoarseness, and the debility of long illness, and the bark and young shoots were occasionally decocted for disorders of the liver and for female complaints [zhenskiye bolezni].

Preparation: Berry oil (maslo oblepikhi): fresh ripe berries are crushed and pressed; the expressed juice is allowed to settle, and the oil layer skimmed from the surface. Applied externally to burns, wounds, and skin ulcerations; also taken internally in doses of one to two spoonfuls [lozhki] per day for cough and debility. Berry decoction: one part dried berries to ten parts water, simmered gently for 20–30 minutes, strained, and drunk warm in small cups [chashki] two to three times daily for digestive and stomach complaints. Leaf or bark decoction: young leaves or bark simmered in water and taken for liver disorders and female ailments.
Indication: ['Burns and scalds', 'Festering or suppurating wounds', 'Skin ulcerations', 'Cough and hoarseness', 'Debility and wasting sickness [iznurenie]', 'Digestive disorders and diarrhoea [ponos]', 'Liver complaints', 'Female complaints [zhenskiye bolezni]']

Original: Облепиха крушиновидная (transliteration: Oblepikha krushinovidnaya) — Hippophae rhamnoides L. [Russian Travnik, 17th–18th century monastery manuscript tradition]
title: Sea Buckthorn (Облепиха крушиновидная) — Monastery and Folk Medicinal Uses

text:
Siberian Ginseng (Eleutherococcus) in Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

Eleutherococcus, known in folk usage as 'wild pepper' [dikiy perets] or 'wind-unfelt' [nechuy-veter], is a shrub native to the forests of Siberia whose root was employed by monastery physicians to restore bodily and spiritual strength, particularly during fasting periods and prolonged prayer vigils. Siberian folk healers [znakhari] prepared decoctions of the root to dispel fatigue and ward off cold ailments, and also steeped tinctures in honey to sustain vigor through the winter months. The plant was regarded as a general restorative [obshcheukreplyayushcheye sredstvo], bridging the Orthodox monastic tradition of medicinal herbs with older Siberian shamanic knowledge of adaptogenic [adaptogennykh] forest plants.

Original: Элеутерококк (Eleutorokok) — Eleutherococcus senticosus. Растение сибирских лесов, именуемое в народе «дикий перец» или «нечуй-ветер». Корень сего кустарника употребляется монастырскими лекарями для укрепления сил телесных и духовных, особливо в пост и при долгих молитвенных бдениях. Сибирские знахари варят отвар из корней для прогнания усталости и хворей простудных; вливают настойку в мёд для поддержания крепости зимою.
title: Siberian Ginseng (Eleutherococcus) in Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

text:
Rhodiola (Golden Root) — Traditional Medicinal Uses in Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Practice

Known in Siberian and Orthodox monastery tradition as 'golden root' [zolotoy koren'], Rhodiola rosea was prized above many simples [prostye lekarstva] for its capacity to restore vital force [zhiznennaya sila] in those weakened by cold, fasting, prolonged labor, or illness. Monastery healers [monakhi-lechtsy] and Siberian folk practitioners alike employed the root to sharpen mental clarity, sustain physical endurance, and calm disordered spirits, a property also recognized in shamanistic use among indigenous Siberian peoples who carried the dried root as a talisman against exhaustion and malevolent influence. Byzantine-derived humoral texts preserved in monastery manuscripts further commend it for warming the 'cold and moist' constitution [kholodnoe i vlazhnoe slozhenie], counteracting melancholy [melanholiya], and supporting the heart and lungs in persons of frail temperament.

Preparation: The dried root [koren'] was prepared most commonly as a cold-water infusion [nastoy na kholodnoy vode] — a small piece of root (approximately one finger-joint's length, roughly 2–3 g by modern measure) steeped overnight in a cup of cold spring water and drunk in the morning on an empty stomach. Warm decoctions [otvar] were also recorded: the root simmered gently for 10–15 minutes in water, then strained and taken in small doses of one to two spoonfuls [lozhki] two or three times daily before meals. Tincture in wine or spirit [nastoyannoe na vine ili spirtnom] was noted for use by travelers and soldiers, taken in very small measure to ward off cold and fatigue. Excessive dose was cautioned against, as overstimulation [izlishneye vozbuzhdenie] was considered a harm to the heart.
Indication: ["General debility and fatigue [obshhaya slabost' i utomlenie]", 'Mental exhaustion and poor concentration', 'Melancholy and disordered spirits [melanholiya]', 'Cold and damp constitutions [kholodnoe slozhenie]', 'Respiratory weakness and shortness of breath', 'Recovery from prolonged illness or fasting', 'Physical endurance during labor, travel, or military campaign']

Original: Родиола розовая (золотой корень) — Rodіola rozovaya (zolotoy koren') — Rhodiola rosea L.
title: Rhodiola (Golden Root) — Traditional Medicinal Uses in Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Practice

text:
Chaga Mushroom — Inonotus obliquus

The chaga mushroom [чага], a hard, blackened conk [древесный нарост] that forms principally upon birch trees in northern forests, was esteemed in Orthodox monastery medicine as a sovereign remedy for ailments of the stomach, bowels, and liver, and was commonly administered to those suffering from prolonged wasting [истощение] or tumorous growths [опухоли]. Siberian folk healers and shamanic practitioners likewise regarded the mushroom as a fortifying agent against malignant disease, prescribing long-boiled decoctions [отвары] to restore vitality and cleanse the blood [очищение крови]. Monastery records further recommend chaga for the relief of pain in the joints [суставные боли], for staunching internal bleeding, and as a general tonic [укрепляющее средство] in cases of chronic debility.

Original: Чага (transliteration: Chaga) — Inonotus obliquus. Source: Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik (травник), 17th–18th century herbal medicine tradition. Slavic folk medicine preserved in monastery manuscripts, blending Byzantine, Central Asian, and native Siberian plant knowledge.
title: Chaga Mushroom — Inonotus obliquus

text:
Scots Pine Resin (Living Resin / Turpentine) — Живица сосновая

Pine resin, called живица ('zhivitsa,' literally 'the living one'), was esteemed in Russian Orthodox monastery medicine for its powerful wound-healing, antimicrobial, and expectorant properties; monastery healers applied it directly to festering wounds, skin ulcers, and burns, believing the resin's vital essence [живительная сила, 'zhivitelnaya sila'] drew out corruption and sealed the flesh. In internal medicine it was administered in small doses for diseases of the chest and lungs — including consumption [чахотка], chronic cough, and bronchial obstruction — as well as for kidney and bladder ailments, being held to cleanse the passages and dissolve [растворять] obstructions. Siberian folk and shamanic traditions additionally employed pine resin fumigations for ritual purification and to ward off illness-bringing spirits, a practice partially absorbed into the monastery dispensary as incense-based inhalation therapy for respiratory complaints.

Preparation: {'raw_topical_application': 'Fresh or softened oleoresin applied directly to wounds, ulcers, and burns as a plaster [пластырь]; sometimes blended with rendered animal fat (bear grease or lard) in a ratio of approximately 1 part resin to 3 parts fat to produce a salve [мазь] for sustained topical use.', 'internal_tincture': 'A small lump of resin (approximately 1–2 zolotnik [золотник], roughly 4–8 g) dissolved in warm rye wine [хлебное вино] or spirit of grain; taken in doses of one small cup (circa 30–50 ml) two to three times daily for lung and kidney complaints.', 'inhalation_fumigation': 'Resin burned on a heated stone or iron plate; the patient inhaled the vapours through a cloth or funnel for bronchial and upper respiratory conditions; adapted in monastery practice as a form of therapeutic censing [каждение].', 'decoction_for_bathing': 'Resin chips or bark pitch simmered in water and used as a wash or sitz bath for skin infections, joint pain [ломота в костях], and rheumatic complaints.'}
Indication: ['Festering wounds, cuts, and skin ulcers', 'Burns', 'Pulmonary consumption [чахотка] and chronic cough', 'Bronchial obstruction and respiratory catarrh', 'Kidney and bladder complaints', 'Rheumatic and joint pain', 'Skin infections and scrofulous eruptions', 'Ritual/prophylactic use against epidemic illness (Siberian shamanic context)']

Original: Живица сосновая (Zhivitsa sosnovaya) — Pinus sylvestris L. [Pine resin / oleoresin; also rendered in monastery sources as 'живица,' lit. 'the living substance' or 'that which gives life']
title: Scots Pine Resin (Living Resin / Turpentine) — Живица сосновая

text:
Garlic (Чеснок посевной) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

Garlic [чеснок посевной] was among the most esteemed medicinal plants in the Russian Orthodox monastery herbal tradition, employed to expel intestinal worms [глисты], purify the blood [очищение крови], and fortify the body against pestilential [чумные] and catarrhal [катаральные] fevers. Monastery physicians prescribed it as a warming [согревающее] and dispersing [рассасывающее] remedy for afflictions of the chest and lungs, including chronic cough, consumption [чахотка], and shortness of breath, drawing on Byzantine humoral doctrine that classified garlic as hot and dry in the fourth degree. In Siberian folk and shamanic practice, garlic was additionally used as a protective [обережное] and fumigatory agent, with cloves burned or hung about the dwelling to ward off malevolent spirits [нечистая сила] and epidemic sickness, a usage recorded alongside Christian blessing rites in several monastery compilations.

Preparation: Raw cloves were crushed and taken internally on an empty stomach, typically 2–3 cloves daily, or macerated in kvass [квас] or honey-water [медовая вода] for milder administration. A decoction [отвар] was prepared by boiling 5–7 crushed cloves in one cup (approximately 240 ml) of water or milk for 10–15 minutes, strained and taken warm in doses of one-third cup [около 80 мл] two to three times daily. For external use against skin parasites and festering wounds [гнойные раны], a poultice [припарка] of crushed raw garlic mixed with lard [свиное сало] or beeswax [пчелиный воск] was applied directly to the affected area and bound with linen cloth.
Indication: ['intestinal parasites (worms) [глисты]', 'pestilential and catarrhal fevers [чумные и катаральные лихорадки]', 'chronic cough and consumption [чахотка]', 'shortness of breath and lung afflictions', 'blood purification [очищение крови]', 'festering wounds and skin parasites', 'epidemic sickness (preventive and fumigatory use)', 'malevolent spiritual influence (shamanic/folk-protective use)']

Original: Чеснок посевной (Chesnoк posevnoy) — Allium sativum L. [Source: Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik (травник), 17th–18th century manuscript tradition]
title: Garlic (Чеснок посевной) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

text:
Horseradish — Traditional Russian Orthodox Monastery Medicinal Uses

Horseradish [khren] was among the most widely employed medicinal roots in Russian Orthodox monastery medicine, valued chiefly for its fierce warming [sogrevaushchee] and dispersing [razgonyaushchee] properties. Monastery healers applied freshly grated root as a poultice to joints afflicted by rheumatic pain, to the chest in cases of lung congestion [zastoy v legkikh], and to the skin to draw out deep cold and damp [kholod i syrост']. In Siberian folk and shamanic practice, a vinegar-macerated preparation of the root was taken internally to expel intestinal parasites, stimulate a sluggish digestion, and as a febrifuge [zharогоnное] during intermittent fevers; the expressed juice, diluted with water, was instilled into the nostrils for chronic catarrh [nasmork khronicheskiy] and sinus obstruction.

Preparation: External: Fresh root grated and applied as a wet poultice [припарка, priparka] directly to affected joints or chest; replaced every 20–30 minutes to prevent skin blistering. Internal: Root sliced and macerated in table vinegar or kvass for 7–10 days; dose of one small spoon [charka, ~15 ml] taken before meals as a digestive and antiparasitic. Nasal wash: Freshly expressed juice diluted 1:3 with warm water, instilled drop-wise for catarrh and sinus congestion. Decoction of grated root in milk was also recorded for chest complaints and persistent cough.
Indication: Rheumatic joint pain; lung congestion and productive cough; intestinal parasites; sluggish digestion and dyspepsia; intermittent fever; chronic nasal catarrh and sinus obstruction; skin conditions treated by counter-irritation [отвлекающее средство].

Original: Хрен обыкновенный (Khren obyknovennyy) — Armoracia rusticana P.Gaertn., B.Mey. & Scherb. Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik (травник), 17th–18th century.
title: Horseradish — Traditional Russian Orthodox Monastery Medicinal Uses

text:
White Mustard (Sinapis alba) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

White mustard [Горчица белая] was employed extensively in Russian Orthodox monastery medicine as a warming and stimulating remedy, applied externally as a poultice [горчичник] to draw blood to the surface of the skin and relieve deep-seated cold and pain in the chest, joints, and lower back. Internally, the seeds were consumed in small quantities to stimulate digestion, expel intestinal worms, and loosen thick [phlegmatic] humours obstructing the lungs and airways — a use consistent with Byzantine humoral theory absorbed into Slavic monastic practice. In Siberian folk contexts, ground mustard was occasionally incorporated into sweat-inducing remedies to break fevers and was applied to the soles of the feet to counter headache and catarrh [насморк], reflecting a blending of Central Asian and native Siberian therapeutic traditions.

Original: Горчица белая (Gorchitsa belaya) — Sinapis alba L. Источник: Русский православный монастырский травник, XVII–XVIII вв.
title: White Mustard (Sinapis alba) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

text:
Cranberry — Traditional Russian Monastery and Folk Medicinal Uses

Cranberry [Клюква, klyukva] was esteemed in Russian Orthodox monastery medicine as a powerful [zharoponizhayushcheye — fever-reducing] and purifying remedy, prescribed chiefly in the treatment of fevers, scorbutic complaints [цинга, tsinga], and ailments of the kidneys and urinary passages. Monastery herbalists prepared the fresh-pressed berry juice [sok] as a restorative drink for monks weakened by fasting, valuing its sharp acidity as a tonic for digestion and a corrective against putrefaction of the blood. In Siberian folk practice — where the plant was gathered from boreal peat bogs — dried berries and their decoctions were additionally employed against sore throats, skin inflammations, and as a general strengthening [ukreplyayushcheye] agent during winter illness.

Preparation: Fresh berries were pressed to yield raw juice [sok], consumed directly as a feverreducing and antiscorbutic drink. Dried berries were simmered in water to produce a decoction [otvar], taken warm in repeated small doses for kidney complaints and throat ailments. Infusions in cooled boiled water were also prepared and used as topical washes for skin inflammation.
Indication: Febrile illness; scurvy [tsinga]; kidney and urinary tract complaints; sore throat and oral inflammation; digestive weakness; general winter debility and convalescent fatigue.

Original: Клюква (Klyukva) — Vaccinium macrocarpon (syn. Oxycoccus macrocarpus). Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik (травник), 17th–18th century manuscript tradition.
title: Cranberry — Traditional Russian Monastery and Folk Medicinal Uses

text:
Rose Hip (Rosa canina) — Russian Monastery Herbal Medicine

The rose hip, known in Russian monastic tradition as Шиповник обыкновенный [Shipovnik obyknovennyy, 'common rose hip'], was among the most revered medicinal plants of the Orthodox monastery herbarium, valued for its fortifying and restorative properties. Monastery physicians [знахари, znakhari] prescribed decoctions of the dried fruits to strengthen the blood, warm the stomach, and expel 'cold humors' [студёные мокроты] from the body, reflecting the blended Byzantine humoral and native Slavic medical frameworks preserved in Travnik manuscripts. In Siberian folk practice, the hips and roots were additionally employed to treat kidney and bladder ailments, suppress fevers, and accelerate wound healing, with some Siberian shamanic traditions attributing protective spiritual properties to the plant.

Preparation: Dried rose hips were typically prepared as a decoction [отвар, otvar]: 2–3 tablespoons of crushed dried fruits simmered in 500 ml of water for 15–20 minutes, then strained and consumed warm, 1–2 cups daily. For kidney and bladder ailments, roots were also decocted similarly. Cold-water infusions [настой, nastoy] of the fruits were employed in warmer seasons. Monastery texts additionally record the preparation of a thick syrup from boiled hips sweetened with honey for administration to the infirm and elderly.
Indication: Fortification of the blood; restoration after illness [convalescence]; digestive weakness and 'cold stomach'; kidney and bladder ailments; febrile illness [fever reduction]; wound healing; general immune strengthening.

Original: Шиповник обыкновенный (Shipovnik obyknovennyy) — Rosa canina L. Source: Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik (травник), 17th–18th century herbal medicine tradition. Context: Slavic folk medicine preserved in monastery manuscripts, blending Byzantine, Central Asian, and native Siberian plant knowledge.
title: Rose Hip (Rosa canina) — Russian Monastery Herbal Medicine

text:
Black Currant (Смородина чёрная) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

The berries, leaves, and buds of black currant were employed in Russian Orthodox monastery medicine as a remedy for colds, coughs, disorders of the kidneys and bladder, scurvy [tsinga], and weakness of the blood [slabost' krovi]. A decoction of the leaves was prepared to purify the blood and strengthen the body, while an infusion of the berries was administered for fever and internal inflammations. Siberian folk healers [znakhari] and monastery physicians alike regarded black currant as a plant possessing the power to fortify the vital spirit [zhiznennaya sila — life force], a belief reflecting the blending of Byzantine humoral theory with native Siberian shamanic traditions.

Preparation: Decoction (отвар, otvar): Fresh or dried leaves simmered in water for 15–20 minutes; administered orally for blood purification and general strengthening. Infusion (настой, nastoy): Dried or fresh berries steeped in hot water for several hours; taken internally for fever reduction and inflammation. Buds (почки, pochki) were sometimes prepared as an alcohol tincture [настойка, nastoyка] in later Travnik practice, particularly for urinary and kidney ailments.
Indication: Scurvy; colds and coughs; fever and acute inflammation; kidney and bladder disorders; blood weakness and general debility; fortification of vital spirit

Original: Смородина чёрная (Smorodina chyornaya) — Ribes nigrum. Ягоды, листья и почки смородины чёрной употребляются в монастырской медицине как средство от простуды, кашля, болезней почек и мочевого пузыря, а также от цинги и слабости крови. Отвар листьев применяется для очищения крови и укрепления тела, а настой ягод — от лихорадки и воспалений. Сибирские знахари и монастырские лекари почитали смородину как растение, обладающее силой укреплять жизненный дух [жизненную силу].
title: Black Currant (Смородина чёрная) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Herbal Medicine

text:
Elderberry (Бузина чёрная) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik

Black elderberry [Бузина чёрная] was among the most esteemed plants in the Russian Orthodox monastery herbal [травник] tradition, valued for its action upon fever, swelling, and disorders of the chest. Monastery healers [лекари] prepared decoctions of the dried flowers and berries to drive out cold humours [хладные мокроты], ease laboured breathing, and provoke a salutary sweat in febrile conditions; bark preparations were employed as a strong purge [слабительное] and to draw off retained waters in cases of dropsy [водянка]. In Siberian and syncretic folk practice, elderberry branches were additionally ascribed protective and apotropaic properties, and infusions of the leaves were applied externally to soothe inflammation of the joints [ломота в костях] and to hasten the ripening and resolution of boils and skin eruptions.

Original: Бузина чёрная (transliteration: Buzina chyornaya) — Sambucus nigra L. [Source: Russian Orthodox Monastery Травник (Travnik), 17th–18th century manuscript tradition, Slavic folk and monastic medicine]
title: Elderberry (Бузина чёрная) — Russian Orthodox Monastery Travnik
